newsitem.title: USA: U.S. court accepts ADM plea, fines.
newsitem.headline: U.S. court accepts ADM plea, fines.

text.p: U.S. District Court Judge Rueben Castillo Tuesday accepted a guilty plea to two counts of price fixing by Archer Daniels Midland Co, and approved a plea agreement that set $100 million in fines.
"This is not a good day for corporate America," Castillo said.
The judge said he recognized that some parties might criticize the fines as not being high enough, but said he believed they would serve as a deterrant to any company that is tempted to fix prices.
"No American company is above the law," Castillo said.

Under the plea agreement accepted by the court, ADM will pay a $70 million fine for fixing prices of lysine, a feed additive, and $30 million for citric acid, an additive used in food, beverages and other products.
Officials from the U.S. Attorney's office said the fine for citric acid was a "downward departure from" -- or a reduction in -- recommended fines because ADM cooperated in this investigation.

Potential fines in the citric acid case could have been high as $224 million, the U.S. Attorney's office said. But officials cautioned that fines would have been limited by the amount of transactions that Justice could prove were affected by alleged price-fixing.
The range of fines in lysine ranged from $54 million to $108 million.

First Assistant U.S. Attorney Scott Lassar told reporters after the hearing that ADM is cooperating in a continuing investigation of possible antitrust activities in high-fructose corn syrup, a sweetener used in foods and beverages. Based on its cooperation, ADM was given immunity in the high fructose corn syrup investigation.

As part of the plea agreement, the U.S. government will not bring criminal charges against any director, officer, or employee of ADM -- with the exception of two top company officials -- in return for their cooperation in ongoing investigations.

As reported earlier, the Justice Department's investigation continues in a price-fixing case against ADM Vice Chairman Michael Andreas and Terrance Wilson, group vice president in charge of corn refining.
Asked why Michael Andreas, son of ADM Chairman Dwayne Andreas, and Wilson were excluded from the plea agreement, Lassar said the arrangement was only with the company.
"The agreement provides for the cooperation of the company and the investigation is continuing. So we will use this cooperation from the company to further that investigation," Lassar said.
